blocks.text:
Design a digital wallet, the system that holds a running balance for each user and lets them transfer money to other users on the same platform instantly, alongside topping up from and withdrawing to the outside world through a bank or card. This category's previous problem, the payment system, solved moving money between a customer and a merchant through an external gateway on every single transaction. This one solves a related but distinct problem: most of its transaction volume, a peer to peer transfer between two wallets the platform itself already holds, never needs to leave the platform at all, and the defining hard problem becomes guaranteeing a wallet's balance can never go negative even when several transfers race to touch it at the exact same time.

The technique that makes concurrent transfers safe without a heavyweight lock on every wallet is optimistic concurrency control, reading a wallet's balance together with a version number, and committing a change only if that version is still unchanged, retrying safely whenever it is not.

blocks.text: A user should be able to transfer money instantly to another user's wallet on the same platform. A user should be able to top up their wallet from an external bank account or card, and withdraw funds back out to one. A wallet's balance should never go negative, regardless of how many transfers are attempted against it concurrently. Funds involved in a pending operation, such as an outgoing withdrawal awaiting external confirmation, should be reserved so they cannot also be spent by an unrelated transfer in the meantime.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the first is the single hardest guarantee the whole design exists to provide.
blocks.content: Five qualities matter here, and the first is the single hardest guarantee the whole design exists to provide.

blocks.alt: No overdrafts ever, fast peer to peer transfers, strong balance consistency, reliability under concurrency, and auditability

blocks.text: No overdrafts ever means a wallet's balance must never go negative, under any concurrent access pattern whatsoever, this is non-negotiable in the same way the payment system's exactly-once charging was. Fast peer to peer transfers means wallet to wallet movement should be dramatically faster than a payment through an external gateway, since it never has to leave the platform. Strong balance consistency means a transfer is atomic, money is never observed missing from one wallet without simultaneously appearing in the other. Reliability under concurrency means two transfers racing against the same wallet at the same instant must both be handled correctly, not just whichever happened to arrive first. And auditability means every balance change has to be traceable back to the exact transfer, top up, or withdrawal that produced it.

blocks.text: This design assumes top ups and withdrawals reuse the payment system's external gateway integration, idempotency keys, and saga pattern directly rather than reinventing them, and focuses instead on what is genuinely new here: internal wallet to wallet transfers and the concurrency control that keeps them safe. Every wallet tracks both an actual balance and a held amount, and a transfer is only permitted against the available balance, actual minus held, covered in section 7. Optimistic concurrency control, not a pessimistic lock per wallet, is assumed as the default concurrency strategy, revisited as a trade-off in section 24.

blocks.text: A digital wallet platform at real scale might hold hundreds of millions of active wallets, with tens of thousands of peer to peer transfers per second at peak. Only a small fraction of wallets ever see genuinely concurrent transfer attempts at the same instant, since most individual wallets are touched by, at most, one transaction at a time, which is exactly what makes optimistic concurrency control, rather than a pessimistic lock on every wallet, the right default. An internal transfer, never leaving the platform, completes in tens of milliseconds, dramatically faster than a payment routed through an external gateway.

blocks.text: A transfer request goes to the wallet service, which reads the sending wallet's balance and version, computes the new balance, and commits it with a compare-and-swap write, crediting the receiving wallet and recording the transfer in an internal ledger, all without ever touching an external gateway. Top ups and withdrawals branch off through the same external payment gateway integration the payment system design already covers. A separate hold service can reserve funds against a wallet's available balance ahead of a pending operation.

blocks.text: Rather than locking a wallet for the duration of every transfer, the wallet service reads its current balance together with a version number, computes the transfer's effect, and commits only if that version is still unchanged at write time. If another operation committed first and changed the version in between, the commit is rejected, and the transfer safely retries against freshly read state.

blocks.alt: A transfer reads the sending wallet's balance and version, commits a compare-and-swap debit, and credits the receiving wallet
A transfer's compare-and-swap attempt is rejected because a concurrent operation already changed the wallet's version, so it re-reads fresh state and retries, succeeding on the second attempt

blocks.text: The happy path is the transfer flow above, a version-checked read, a successful compare-and-swap debit, and a credit to the other side. The workflow worth walking through separately is the concurrency retry flow, where some other operation, another transfer, a top up, anything touching that same wallet, commits in the narrow window between this transfer's read and its own commit attempt. Rather than either overwriting that concurrent change or blocking behind a lock, the transfer's compare-and-swap simply fails, and the wallet service transparently retries against freshly read state, which is what lets the design avoid a pessimistic lock on every single wallet while still never risking an overdraft.

from typing import Dict, Optional


# The outcome of a transfer attempt, including how many compare-and-swap
# attempts it took to commit, to make the retry behavior visible.
class TransferResult:
    def __init__(self, status: str, attempts_used: int):
        self.status = status
        self.attempts_used = attempts_used


# One wallet's durable state: its actual balance, any amount currently held
# for a pending operation, and a version number used for optimistic concurrency.
class Wallet:
    def __init__(self, balance: int):
        self.balance = balance   # the true, settled balance
        self.held = 0               # funds reserved for a pending operation, not spendable
        self.version = 0              # incremented on every committed balance-changing write


# Manages wallets with optimistic concurrency control: every balance-changing
# write reads a version number and commits only if it is still unchanged,
# retrying against fresh state whenever a concurrent update wins the race.
class WalletService:
    def __init__(self):
        self._wallets: Dict[str, Wallet] = {}
        self._pending_race_wallet_id: Optional[str] = None   # one-shot hook, armed by debug_inject_concurrent_update_once
        self._pending_race_amount = 0

    def create_wallet(self, wallet_id: str, initial_balance: int) -> None:
        self._wallets[wallet_id] = Wallet(initial_balance)

    def actual_balance(self, wallet_id: str) -> int:
        return self._wallets[wallet_id].balance

    # Available balance is what a transfer is actually checked against, never
    # the actual balance alone, so held funds can never be double spent.
    def available_balance(self, wallet_id: str) -> int:
        wallet = self._wallets[wallet_id]
        return wallet.balance - wallet.held

    def place_hold(self, wallet_id: str, amount: int) -> None:
        self._wallets[wallet_id].held += amount   # reserve funds, reducing available balance without touching actual balance

    def release_hold(self, wallet_id: str, amount: int) -> None:
        self._wallets[wallet_id].held -= amount   # release the reservation, restoring available balance

    # Arms a one-time simulated concurrent update, purely to deterministically
    # demonstrate the compare-and-swap retry path in this single-threaded demo;
    # in production this same conflict would arise naturally from real concurrent requests.
    def debug_inject_concurrent_update_once(self, wallet_id: str, simulated_concurrent_top_up: int) -> None:
        self._pending_race_wallet_id = wallet_id
        self._pending_race_amount = simulated_concurrent_top_up

    # Transfers amount from from_wallet_id to to_wallet_id using optimistic concurrency
    # control: reads balance and version, then commits only if the version is
    # still unchanged, retrying with fresh state on a version mismatch.
    def transfer(self, from_wallet_id: str, to_wallet_id: str, amount: int) -> TransferResult:
        attempts = 0
        while True:
            attempts += 1
            from_wallet = self._wallets[from_wallet_id]
            seen_version = from_wallet.version                              # the version this attempt is based on
            available = from_wallet.balance - from_wallet.held                 # available balance at the moment of this read

            if available < amount:
                return TransferResult("DENIED_INSUFFICIENT_AVAILABLE_BALANCE", attempts)

            # Deterministically simulate a concurrent update landing between this
            # read and this attempt's own commit, exactly once, if armed.
            if from_wallet_id == self._pending_race_wallet_id:
                from_wallet.balance += self._pending_race_amount   # some other operation's change, already committed
                from_wallet.version += 1                              # its own version bump
                self._pending_race_wallet_id = None                     # fire only once

            committed = self._compare_and_swap_debit(from_wallet_id, seen_version, amount)
            if committed:
                self._credit_wallet(to_wallet_id, amount)
                return TransferResult("SUCCESS", attempts)
            # Version mismatch: someone else committed first. Loop and retry with fresh state.

    def _compare_and_swap_debit(self, wallet_id: str, expected_version: int, amount: int) -> bool:
        wallet = self._wallets[wallet_id]
        if wallet.version != expected_version:
            return False   # the version changed since this attempt's read; reject, caller will retry
        wallet.balance -= amount   # commit the debit
        wallet.version += 1           # advance the version so any other concurrent attempt now correctly fails
        return True

    def _credit_wallet(self, wallet_id: str, amount: int) -> None:
        wallet = self._wallets[wallet_id]
        wallet.balance += amount
        wallet.version += 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    wallet_service = WalletService()
    wallet_service.create_wallet("wallet-A", 1000)
    wallet_service.create_wallet("wallet-B", 500)

    # A normal transfer with no contention and no holds in the way.
    first = wallet_service.transfer("wallet-A", "wallet-B", 300)
    print(f"Transfer 1: {first.status}, attempts={first.attempts_used}")
    print(f"  wallet-A balance={wallet_service.actual_balance('wallet-A')} available={wallet_service.available_balance('wallet-A')}")
    print(f"  wallet-B balance={wallet_service.actual_balance('wallet-B')}")

    # Place a hold on wallet-A, e.g. for a pending withdrawal, reducing its available balance.
    wallet_service.place_hold("wallet-A", 500)
    print(f"After a 500 hold, wallet-A available balance={wallet_service.available_balance('wallet-A')} (actual balance is still {wallet_service.actual_balance('wallet-A')})")

    # This transfer should be denied: available balance (200) is less than the requested 300,
    # even though the actual balance (700) alone would be enough.
    second = wallet_service.transfer("wallet-A", "wallet-B", 300)
    print(f"Transfer 2 (should be denied): {second.status}")

    # Release the hold, restoring wallet-A's available balance.
    wallet_service.release_hold("wallet-A", 500)
    print(f"After releasing the hold, wallet-A available balance={wallet_service.available_balance('wallet-A')}")

    # Simulate a genuinely concurrent update landing between this transfer's read and its
    # own compare-and-swap commit attempt, e.g. a top up processed by another thread.
    wallet_service.debug_inject_concurrent_update_once("wallet-A", 100)
    third = wallet_service.transfer("wallet-A", "wallet-B", 300)
    print(f"Transfer 3 (hits one simulated version conflict, then retries): {third.status}, attempts={third.attempts_used}")
    print(f"  wallet-A final balance={wallet_service.actual_balance('wallet-A')}")
    print(f"  wallet-B final balance={wallet_service.actual_balance('wallet-B')}")

items: Architecture: internal wallet to wallet transfers via optimistic concurrency control against a versioned balance store, with top ups and withdrawals branching through the payment system's external gateway integration.
Capacity: hundreds of millions of active wallets, tens of thousands of peer to peer transfers per second at peak, with genuine concurrency affecting only a small fraction of wallets.

The core techniques: an available-versus-actual balance model with holds, and optimistic concurrency control with a compare-and-swap retry loop, both worked through with a real, verified implementation.
Database: a versioned, wallet-id-partitioned balance store as the strongly consistent source of truth, alongside an append-only transfer ledger for auditability.
End-to-end workflows: a normal transfer and a version-conflict retry, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: strongly consistent actual and available balances for every real transfer decision, with only display-layer caching allowed any lag at all.

Trade-offs: optimistic concurrency control versus pessimistic per-wallet locking versus no concurrency control at all, compared directly on uncontended cost, behavior under contention, and where each breaks down.
